title: From One Egg to Organized Tissues

scenes.visual: Title card: From One Egg to Organized Tissues. Show a schematic layered embryo with distinct outer, middle and inner layers.

scenes.tts: How does one fertilized egg become a body? Gastrulation organizes the embryo into layers that make different tissues. Cells move from the surface to the inside and sort into germ layers. Most animals form three: ectoderm outside, mesoderm in the middle, and endoderm inside. In vertebrates, ectoderm makes epidermis and nervous tissue. Mesoderm makes muscle and blood. Endoderm makes the gut and airway lining. Arranging the cells sets up where different body tissues will develop.
scenes.visual: Open on the question, then immediately show surface cells moving inward into a schematic three-layer embryo. Label ectoderm outside, mesoderm in the middle and endoderm inside. Identify the tissue examples as vertebrate examples: connect each layer to epidermis/nervous tissue, muscle/blood, or gut/airway epithelium. Keep layer colours consistent throughout.

scenes.tts: The movements differ. In invagination, a sheet bends inward. In involution, it rolls over an edge and spreads inside. In ingression, single cells leave a sheet and move inward. Germ layers make tissues, not whole organs. An intestine has endoderm lining, with mesoderm muscle and connective tissue around it. Neural crest cells from ectoderm add nerve cells.
scenes.visual: Replace the doubling counter with three labelled movement diagrams: a sheet bending inward, a sheet rolling over an edge and spreading inside, and individual cells leaving a sheet. Then show an intestinal cross-section: endoderm-derived epithelial lining, mesoderm-derived muscle and connective tissue, and ectoderm-derived neural crest nerve cells.

scenes.tts: What tells a cell what to become? Both what it inherits and signals it receives. Cytoplasmic determinants are molecules placed in regions of the egg and inherited by cells there. Induction is a signal from one group of cells that changes the fate of neighbours. The amphibian organizer shows this: a graft recruited host cells into a second body axis. Most embryos studied closely use both inherited factors and induction.
scenes.visual: Replace the volume check with two inputs to cell fate: molecules inherited from a region of egg cytoplasm, and a signal arriving from neighbouring cells. Show a schematic amphibian organizer graft recruiting host cells into a second body axis; distinguish graft cells from recruited host cells. Finish with both inputs converging on cell fate.

scenes.tts: Earlier, cleavage supplies the cells. After fertilization, the egg divides into smaller cells without growing. Each is a blastomere. Yolk slows or blocks the cleavage furrow. In birds, only a disc of cytoplasm on top of the yolk divides.
scenes.visual: Mark the transition as Earlier: cleavage, to make the shift in time explicit. Replace diameter bars with a constant-size egg outline partitioning into smaller blastomeres. Then show a bird egg with a divided disc above an undivided yolk mass. Omit all spherical diameter and membrane-area calculations.

scenes.tts: Fertilization starts the process. Sperm and egg fuse to form a zygote. A calcium wave activates the egg and restarts the cell cycle. Eggs also block extra sperm. In mice, reviews conclude the membrane block is not electrical.
scenes.visual: Move further back in time, labelled Starting event: fertilization. Replace membrane-area bars with sperm-egg fusion, then a calcium wave crossing the egg and a cell-cycle restart. Show additional sperm blocked outside. Label the mouse membrane block as non-electrical; do not depict an electrical barrier for the mouse.

scenes.tts: Now follow one tissue forward. In frogs, birds and mammals, the neural plate folds into a hollow neural tube, the future brain and spinal cord. Neural crest forms at the plate edges and makes peripheral neurons and much of the skeleton of the face and skull.
scenes.visual: Transition to a vertebrate tissue example, labelled Frogs, birds and mammals. Show a neural plate of ectoderm folding and pinching off into a hollow neural tube. Label future brain and spinal cord. Highlight neural crest at the plate edges, then connect it to peripheral neurons and much of the facial/skull skeleton. Keep the ectoderm colour used at the opening.
